_note: Handling windows are the estimated maximum time at ambient tropical temperature (~28-32 C) before significant quality loss, based on sources cited in each 'source' field. Values represent unrefrigerated short-haul dispatch windows, not cold-chain shelf life.

commodities.name: kangkung
commodities.source: FAO (2005) 'Quality and safety in the traditional horticultural marketing chains of Asia', p.18: leafy vegetables at tropical ambient lose marketable quality within 6 h without shade/moisture.

commodities.name: bayam
commodities.source: FAO (2005) ibid. p.18: same category as kangkung; both are high-respiration tropical leafy crops.

commodities.name: tomat
commodities.source: Kader, A.A. (ed.) (2002) Postharvest Technology of Horticultural Crops, 3rd ed., UC Davis ANR Pub. 3311, p.279: ripe tomatoes at 20 C retain acceptable quality ~1-2 days (24-48 h); 24 h used as conservative ambient tropical dispatch limit.

commodities.name: cabai
commodities.source: Kader (2002) p.268: chilli peppers at 20-25 C show visible quality loss within 2-4 days ambient; 48 h used as conservative dispatch limit.

commodities.name: kubis
commodities.source: Kader (2002) p.239: cabbage at 20 C retains quality 3-7 days; 72 h (3 days) used as conservative ambient dispatch limit.

commodities.name: wortel
commodities.source: Kader (2002) p.243: carrots at 20 C typically acceptable 4-7 days; 96 h (4 days) used as conservative ambient dispatch limit.

commodities.name: kentang
commodities.source: Kader (2002) p.290: potatoes stored dry and dark at 20 C acceptable quality for 2-4 weeks; 168 h (7 days) used as conservative short-haul dispatch limit.

commodities.name: bawang merah
commodities.source: FAO (1993) 'Prevention of post-harvest food losses: fruits, vegetables and root crops', FAO Training Series No.17/2, p.52: dry-cured shallots acceptable 2-4 weeks at ambient; 336 h (14 days) used as dispatch limit.
